newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban doubt Afghan opposition sincerity in talks.
newsitem.headline: Taleban doubt Afghan opposition sincerity in talks.

text.p: The most senior member of the Taleban administration in Kabul said on Wednesday he doubted that talks between the Taleban and opposition groups would succeed since the opposition was not sincere.

"We are willing to take part in any peaceful negotiations, but I personally think that they will not be successful because the other side is insincere," Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, head of the Taleban interim ruling council, told Reuters.

"The experience of the last three years has shown that whenever there have been negotiations for a peaceful solution to the Afghan crisis, it has reached a stage where the enemy have regrouped and reinforced before launching an offensive," said Rabbani.
The United Nations hopes to start a second round of talks beween the warring Afghan factions in the Pakistani capital Islamabad soon.
The United Nations describes the talks as "technical level discussions" about the preliminary stages of a peaceful solution.
Rabbani said the Taleban were still willing to negotiate with the opposition, whom he accused of looting the country, but that time was running out.

"We once again would like to offer negotiations to those who have looted the treasury and opposed the Islamic government (the Taleban). We are ready for talks but if they do not accept this offer, the nation will rise against them," he said.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul last September, control more than two thirds of Afghanistan and face the opposition on front lines north of Kabul and in the remote northwestern provinces of the country.
The opposition is made up of former government forces allied with northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite leader Karim Khalili.
Rabbani reiterated an offer of amnesty to opposition commanders who defected to the Taleban.
"Enemy commanders who surrender to the Islamic Army will be welcomed and treated according to Islamic principles," he said.
But he was less forgiving when asked if the amnesty included opposition leaders such as General Dostum and Ahmed Shah Masood, the commander of the former government troops.
"This question can be raised when they surrender and repent of their former deeds. Then whatever decision is made by the nation based on Islamic principles will be implemented," he said.
Rabbani called the lack of international recognition for the Taleban unfair.

"Except for some parts of the country where we don't have access, we have established peace and security but still the world does not recognise us. This is unfair. It is our legal right to be recognised." he said.

The Taleban have yet to be recognised as the legal authorities in Afghanistan by any nation or international organisation. The question of recognition is not expected to be discussed in the U.N. General Assembly before October.
Rabbani pointed out that the former government had obtained international recognition when it controlled substantially less of the country than the Taleban did now.
"It is very strange for us that they recognised the former regime when they didn't even have control of the capital, let alone the rest of the country," he said.
Afghanistan's seat in the United Nations is occupied by a representative of the former government.
